summary: Another revision of the Network Working Group's documentation conventions, updating RFC 10, RFC 16 and RFC 24. It restates how notes in the series are produced and shared. A later revision appears in RFC 30.

plainLanguage.summary: This note sets out the simple rules for the group's written notes. Anyone may write one, rough ideas are welcome, and the note explains the header and who receives a copy.

questions: what was the network working group
what are the rfc documentation conventions
subtitle: The early rules for writing Network Working Group notes: short, informal, open to anyone, and mailed to a fixed list.

tldr.problem: The Network Working Group wanted to document its work on HOST software and network strategy, but people held back from publishing rough or unfinished ideas.
tldr.mechanism: Anyone may write a note on any network topic. Each note carries a fixed header (serial number, author, date, title) and one copy goes to each of 12 named people.
tldr.outcome: The note revises RFC 10, RFC 16 and RFC 24, and was itself updated by RFC 30.

sections.title: The Group and Its Notes
sections.content:
This note revises RFC 10, RFC 16 and RFC 24. The Network Working Group (NWG) consists of interested people from existing or potential ARPA network sites, and membership is not closed. It is concerned with the HOST software, the strategies for using the network, and early experience with the network.

The group documents its work through notes such as this one. A note may be produced at any site by anybody and included in the series.
sections.plainLanguage: The group is an open club of people who build software for the network. It writes short notes to share its work, and anyone at any site may write one.

sections.title: What a Note May Contain
sections.content:
A note may hold any thought or suggestion related to the HOST software or another aspect of the network. Notes are encouraged to be timely rather than polished. Philosophical positions without examples, specific suggestions without background, and questions without attempted answers are all acceptable, and the minimum length for a note is one sentence.

The RFC states these loose standards for two reasons. First, a written statement tends to be seen as authoritative, and the group wants to encourage discussion of far less authoritative ideas. Second, people naturally hesitate to publish something unpolished, and the group wants to ease that hesitation.
sections.plainLanguage: A note may be any idea about the network, however unfinished. Even a single sentence counts, so no one should feel that their idea is too rough to share.

sections.title: The Required Form
sections.content: Every note should carry four items. The first is the words Network Working Group and Request for Comments: X, where X is a serial number assigned by Steve Crocker at UCLA. The others are the author and affiliation, the date, and a title. The title need not be unique.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note needs four things: a serial number, who wrote it and where they work, the date, and a name. The name does not have to be the only one of its kind.

sections.title: Distribution
sections.content: The author's site sends one copy to each of 12 named people, at MIT, Utah, SDC, UCLA, SRI, MITRE, RAND, BB&N, Raytheon, ARPA, Lincoln Laboratory and UCSB. Further reproduction may be handled locally. The note also lists the current addresses and phone numbers for each person and asks recipients to correct them where necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: The writer mails one copy to each of twelve people. Each of them can make more copies locally if needed. The note also lists everyone's address so it can be corrected.

references.text: Documentation conventions, NWG/RFC 10, revised by this note.
